¶
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To happen; come to pass.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have reveal’d . . .
The discord which ''befell.'' ''Milton'', P. L., vi. 897.</poem>
<poem>The ground in many a little dell
Was broken, up and down whose steeps ''befell''
Alternate victory and defeat.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Revolt of Islam, vi. 16.}}}}

'''2†.''' To fall in the way; come to hand.
{{smaller block|<poem>His little Goats gan drive out of their stalls,
To feede abroad, where pasture best ''befalls.''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Virgil’s Gnat, l. 72.}}}}

'''To befall of†''', to be the fate of; become of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Do me the favour to dilate at full
What hath ''befall’n of'' them, and thee, till now.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1.}}}}

¶
'''befana''' (be-fä′nạ̈), ''n.'' [It., < ''befania'', epiphany, < LL. ''epiphania'', epiphany: see ''Epiphany''.] '''1.''' Primarily, in Italy, an Epiphany present or gift.—'''2.''' [''cap.''] The witch or fairy said to bring children the sweetmeats and other rewards given them on the eve of Epiphany, or to neglect and punish them.
{{smaller block|In nursery parlance the ''Befana'' has two aspects; she not only brings gifts to good children, but is the terror of the naughty. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 6th ser., IX. 422.}}}}
'''3.''' A large rag doll, representing the Befana, placed on the chimneys of cottages, etc., or displayed in shops, in Italy, where Epiphany gifts are sold, for the terror or amusement of children. {{smaller|[The above meanings and customs have reference to the gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Mat. ii. 11) brought by the Magi to the child Jesus, which the feast of the Epiphany commemorates. The grotesque blackened figures often exhibited are explained by the tradition that one of the three wise kings was an Ethi-}}

'''befetter''' (bē-fet′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fetter.''] To confine with fetters; restrain as if by fetters.
{{smaller block|Tongue-tied, ''befettered'', heavy-laden nations.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. i. 10.}}}}

'''beffroi†''', ''n.'' [F.] See ''belfry.''

'''beffroy†''', ''n.'' In ''her.'', same as ''vair.''

''befȳlan'', < ''be-'' + ''fȳlan'', file, foul, < ''fūl'', foul: see ''file''<sup>2</sup>, ''foul''<sup>1</sup>, and ''befoul'', and cf. ''defile''<sup>1</sup>.] To make filthy; befoul; soil.

'''befit''' (bē-fit′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befitted'', ppr. ''befitting.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fit.''] '''1.''' To suit; be suitable to; become.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dry up your tears,
Which ill ''befit'' the beauty of that face.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 3.}}
<poem>Out of my sight, thou serpent! That name best
''Befits'' thee.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 868.}}

{{right|''Drayton'', Barons’ Wars, iv.}}}}
'''2†.''' To fit; furnish with something fit. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He . . . had seriously ''befitted'' him with just such a bridle and such a saddle.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy.}}}}

'''befell''' (bē-fel′). Preterit of ''befall.''

'''befetter''' (bē-fet′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fetter.'']   To confine with fetters; restrain as if by fetters.
{{smaller block|Tongue-tied, ''befettered'', heavy-laden nations.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. i. 10.}}}}

'''beffroy†''', ''n.'' In ''her.'', same as ''vair.''

'''befile†''', ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E. also ''befyle'', < ME. ''befylen'', ''befilen'' (mixed with ''befulen'', ''befoulen'', which rest directly upon ''ful'', ''foul'', foul), < AS. ''befȳlan'', < ''be-'' + ''fȳlan'', file, foul, < ''fūl'', foul: see ''file''<sup>2</sup>, ''foul''<sup>1</sup>, and ''befoul'', and cf. ''defile''<sup>1</sup>.]   To make filthy; befoul; soil.

'''befit''' (bē-fit′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befitted'', ppr. ''befitting.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fit.'']   '''1.''' To suit; be suitable to; become.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dry up your tears,
Which ill ''befit'' the beauty of that face.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Out of my sight, thou serpent! That name best
''Befits'' thee.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 868.}}}}
{{smaller block|Robes ''befitting'' his degree.
{{right|''Drayton'', Barons’ Wars, iv.}}}}

{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy.}}}}

'''befitting''' (bē-fit′ing), ''p. a.'' Of a suitable kind or character; fit; proper; becoming: as, ''befitting'' words; a ''befitting'' dress or manner.

'''befittingly''' (bẹ̄-fit′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a befitting or appropriate manner; becomingly.

'''beflea''' (bẹ̄-flē′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''flea''<sup>1</sup>.]   To pester, as fleas do.
{{smaller block|<poem>One of those bores
Who ''beflea’d'' with bad verses poor Louis Quatorze.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Fable for Critics.}}}}

'''beflecked''' (bẹ̄-flekt′), ''a.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''flecked.'']   Flecked; spotted or streaked; variegated. Also spelled ''befleckt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Dark billows of an earthquake storm
''Beflecked'' with clouds like foam.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Hill-top.}}}}

'''beflower''' (bẹ̄-flou′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''flower.'']   To cover or besprinkle with flowers.
{{smaller block|Beside a ''beflowered'' and garlanded precipice.
{{right|''S. L. Clemens'', Life on the Mississippi, p. 274.}}}}

'''beflum''' (bẹ̄-flum′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beflummed'', ppr. ''beflumming.''   [Sc.; also in the appar. perverted forms ''bleflum, blaflum, blephum, v.'' and ''n.'', perhaps < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + *''flum'', as in ''flummery'', or a variant of ''flam.'' Words of this kind are very unstable.]   To befool by cajoling language; flatter.   ''Scott.'' [Scotch.]

'''befoam''' (bẹ̄-fōm′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''foam.'']   To cover with foam.   ''Dryden.''

'''befog''' (bẹ̄-fog′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befogged'', ppr. ''befogging.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fog.'']   To involve in fog; hence, figuratively, to confuse; make obscure or uncertain; bewilder: as, to ''befog'' the mind with sophistry.

{{smaller block|Intentional and persistent efforts have been . . . made to ''befog'' the whole subject.
{{right|''D. A. Wells'', Merchant Marine, p. 120.}}}}

'''befool''' (bē̤-föl′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''befolen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fool''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To make a fool of; delude; dupe.
{{smaller block|<poem>I could burst with rage,
To think I have a brother so ''befool’d.''</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Love’s Sacrifice, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To treat as a fool; call (a person) “fool.”

'''before''' (bē̤-fōr′), ''adv.'', ''prep.'', and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''beforen'', ''beforn'', ''biforen'', ''biforn'', etc., adv. and prep., < AS. ''beforan'', ''biforan'', adv. and prep., before (in place or time: in the latter use rare, the ordinary word being ''ǣr'', ere) (= OS. ''biforan'' = D. ''bevoren'' = OHG. ''bifora'', MHG. ''bevor'', ''bevorn'', G. ''bevor''), < ''be'', by, about, + ''foran'', adv., before, < ''for'', for, lit. before: see ''fore'' and ''for'', and cf. ''afore''.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' In front; on the anterior or fore side; on the side opposite the back; in a position or at a point in advance; ahead.
{{smaller block|The battle was ''before'' and behind.
{{right|2 Chron. xiii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|Reaching forth unto those things which are ''before.''
{{right|Phil. iii. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|Had he his hurts ''before?''
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I am sent with broom ''before'',
To sweep the dust behind the door.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|If you will walk ''before'', sir, I will overtake you instantly.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' In time preceding; previously; formerly; already.
{{smaller block|You tell me what I knew ''before.''
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|A flatterer is a dunce to him, for he can tell him nothing but what hee knowes ''before.'' {{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, A Selfe-conceited Man.}}}}

[The adverb is frequently used in self-explaining compounds, as ''before-cited'', ''before-going'', ''before-mentioned'', etc.]

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' In front of, in time or position; on the anterior or fore side of; in a position or at a point in advance of: as, a happy future lies ''before'' you; ''before'' the house; ''before'' the fire.
{{smaller block|The golden age, which a blind tradition has hitherto placed in the Past, is ''before'' us.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Before'' them went the priest reading the burial service.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Twice-Told Tales, I.}}}}
'''2.''' In presence of; in sight of; under the cognizance, jurisdiction, or consideration of.
{{smaller block|Abraham bowed down himself ''before'' the people of the land.
{{right|Gen. xxiii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They tell me, if they might be brought ''before'' you,
They would reveal things of strange consequence.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Sea Voyage, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If my lady die,
I’ll be sworn ''before'' a jury, thou art the cause on ’t.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Scornful Lady, v. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' In precedence of; in advance of, as regards rank, condition, development, etc.
{{smaller block|He that cometh after me is preferred ''before'' me.
{{right|John i. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|I can shew one almost of the same nature, but much ''before'' it.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The eldest son is ''before'' the younger in succession.
{{right|''Johnson.''}}}}
'''4.''' In preference to; rather than.
<poem>One joyous howre in blisfull happines,
I chose ''before'' a life of wretchednes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 984.}}}}

{{smaller block|I love my friend ''before'' myself.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, ii. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|We think poverty to be infinitely desirable ''before'' the torments of covetousness.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor''.}}}}
'''5.''' Anterior to in time; previous to: as, I shall return ''before'' six o’clock.

{{smaller block|Temple sprang from a family which, though ancient and honourable, had ''before'' his time been scarcely mentioned in our history.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir William Temple.}}}}

{{smaller block|They arrived close to Alhama about two hours ''before'' daybreak.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 30.}}}}
'''6.''' Under the action, influence, or power of.

{{smaller block|Mordecai, . . . ''before'' whom thou hast begun to fall.
{{right|Esther vi. 13.}}}}

{{smaller block|Tower and town, as he advanced, went down ''before'' him.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Before all.''' See ''all''.—'''Before the beam''' (''naut.''), in a position or direction which lies before a line drawn at right angles to the keel at the midship section of the ship.—'''Before''' (or '''afore''') '''the mast,''' as a common sailor, the crew of a ship being berthed in the forecastle or forward of the foremast.—'''Before the wind.''' (''a'') ''Naut.'', in the direction of the wind: as, to sail ''before the wind'', that is, in the direction in which the wind blows: said of a ship.}}

{{smaller block|We continued running dead ''before the wind'', knowing that we sailed better so.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 20.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') Figuratively and colloquially, in prosperous circumstances; out of debt or difficulty.}}

'''III.''' ''conj.'' '''1.''' Previous to the time when: formerly sometimes followed by ''that''.

{{smaller block|''Before'' I was afflicted, I went astray.
{{right|Ps. cxix. 67.}}}}

{{smaller block|Jesus answered and said unto him, ''Before that'' Philip called thee . . . I saw thee. {{right|John i. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Before'' this treatise can be of use, two points are necessary. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Seventy of the Moors made their way into the streets ''before'' an alarm was given. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' Sooner than; rather than.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then take my soul; my body, soul, and all,
''Before'' that England give the French the foil.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3.}}}}

'''beforehand''' (bē-fōr′hand), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''beforehond'', ''bifornhand'', ''bivorenhond'', before, previously, < ''beforen'', before, + ''hand'', ''hond'', hand.]   '''1.''' In anticipation; in advance.
{{smaller block|So that they . . . may be taught ''beforehand'' the skill of speaking. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
'''2†.''' Before there is time for anything to be done; before anything is done.
{{smaller block|What is a man’s contending with insuperable difficulties but the rolling of Sisyphus’s stone up the hill, which is soon ''beforehand'' to return upon him again? {{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''To be beforehand with,''' to anticipate; be in advance of; be prepared or ready for.}}
{{smaller block|Agricola . . . resolves ''to be beforehand with'' the danger. {{right|''Milton.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The last-cited author has been ''beforehand with'' me. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}

'''beforehand''' (bē-fōr′hand), ''a.''   [< ''beforehand'', ''adv.'' Cf. ''forehanded.'']   In good pecuniary circumstances; having enough to meet one’s obligations and something over; forehanded: as, “rich and much ''beforehand'',” ''Bacon.'' [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|I now began to think of getting a little ''beforehand.'' {{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., p. 77.}}}}

'''beforesaid''' (bē-fōr′sed), ''a.'' Aforesaid.   ''Chaucer.''

'''beforetime''' (bē-fōr′tīm), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''beforetyme''; < ''before'' + ''time.'' Cf. ''aforetime.'']   Formerly; of old time; aforetime. [Obsolescent.]
{{smaller block|''Beforetime'' in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake.
{{right|1 Sam. ix. 9.}}}}

'''befortune†''' (bẹ̄-fôr′tụ̄n), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fortune.'']   To happen; betide.
{{smaller block|I wish all good ''befortune'' you. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 3.}}}}

'''befoul''' (bē-foul′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''befoulen'', ''befulen'' (mixed with ''befylen'', etc.: see ''befile''), < ''be-'' + ''foulen'', foul: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''foul''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   To make foul; cover with filth; soil; tarnish.
{{smaller block|Lawyers can live without ''befouling'' each other’s names.
{{right|''Trollope'', Barchester Towers, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Birds of prey winged their way to the stately tree, ''befouling'' its purity.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXVI. 263.}}}}

'''befreckle''' (bẹ̄-frek′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''freckle.'']   To freckle; spot; color with various spots; variegate.
{{smaller block|Her star-''befreckled'' face. {{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xxii. 910.}}}}

'''befret''' (bē-fret′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befretted'', ppr. ''befretting''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fret''<sup>1</sup>.]   To fret or gnaw away.
{{smaller block|<poem>Accept this ring, wherein my heart is set,
A constant heart with burning flames ''befret.''</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', James IV., iv.}}}}

'''befriend''' (bē-frend′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''friend.'']   To act as a friend to; countenance, aid, or benefit; assist; favor: as, fortune ''befriended'' me.
{{smaller block|That you were once unkind, ''befriends'' me now.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxx.}}}}
{{smaller block|The climate [of Chæronea] is not much ''befriended'' by the heavens, for the air is thick and foggy.
{{right|''Dryden'', Life of Plutarch.}}}}
{{smaller block|Every little pine needle expanded and swelled with sympathy and ''befriended'' me. {{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 143.}}}}

'''befriendment''' (bẹ̄-frend′ment), ''n.''   [< ''befriend'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of befriending.   ''Foster.'' [Rare.]

'''befrill''' (bẹ̄-fril′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''frill''.]   To furnish or deck with a frill or frills.
{{smaller block|The vicar’s white-haired mother, ''befrilled'' . . . with dainty cleanliness. {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xvii.}}}}

'''befringe''' (bẹ̄-frinj′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fringe''.]   To furnish with a fringe; adorn as with fringe.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let my dirty leaves . . .
''Befringe'' the rails of Bedlam and Soho.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, II. i. 419.}}}}

'''befriz''' (bẹ̄-friz′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befrizzed'', ppr. ''befrizzing''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''friz''.]   To curl the hair of; friz.
{{smaller block|''Befrizzed'' and bepowdered courtiers.
{{right|''Contemporary Rev.''}}}}

'''befuddle''' (bẹ̄-fud′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fuddle''.]   To stupefy or muddle with intoxicants; make stupidly drunk.

'''befur''' (bẹ̄-fėr′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''befurred'', ppr. ''befurring''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fur''.]   '''1.''' To cover or supply with fur.—'''2†.''' To fur over; incrust.   ''N. E. D.''

'''beg'''<sup>1</sup> (beg), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''begged'', ppr. ''begging''.   [Early mod. E. also ''begg'', ''begge'', < ME. ''beggen'', first found in the early part of the 13th century (in the “Ancren Riwle”); origin un-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
